lines: So Moses the servant of Yahweh died there in the land of Moab. He buried him in the valley, opposite Beth Peor. But no man knows where his tomb is, to this day.
That's the end of Deuteronomy, the fifth book of the Bible. And for more than two thousand years, the tradition said Moses wrote all five books.
Including, apparently, his own death. And his own burial. And the words: to this day.
Genesis. Exodus. Leviticus. Numbers. Deuteronomy. In Hebrew, the Torah. Jews and Christians alike called them the Five Books of Moses.
Even the tradition noticed the problem. One opinion in the Talmud says Joshua wrote the last eight verses, the ones after Moses dies. Another says Moses wrote them himself, in tears.
In the twelfth century, the scholar Abraham ibn Ezra hinted, in careful code, at other lines that looked like they came from a later time.
By the sixteen hundreds, Thomas Hobbes and Baruch Spinoza said it out loud. Moses could not have written all of this.
The first systematic method came from a French physician. In 1753, Jean Astruc used the two different names Genesis gives God to sort it into older documents.
Sometimes God is Elohim, the ordinary Hebrew word for God. Sometimes he is Yahweh: the personal name, four Hebrew letters, which Jewish tradition does not pronounce aloud.
And the names cluster. Here is every use of both words, chapter by chapter, through Genesis. Whole stretches lean one way, then the other.
Astruc was a believer. He thought Moses had worked from older documents. But he had found a seam.
You can see it on the first page.
Genesis chapter one. Elohim creates in six days, and rests on the seventh. Plants. Then animals. Then humans, male and female together, last of all.
Then chapter two starts over. Now it's Yahweh God. He forms a man from the dust first. Then he plants a garden. Then he makes the animals. Only then, the woman.
A different name. A different order. A different picture of God. One speaks the world into being. The other shapes a man from the dust, and breathes into his nostrils.
Once you start looking, the doubles are everywhere.
Three times, a patriarch passes off his wife as his sister. Twice, Hagar ends up in the wilderness, and twice an angel finds her there. Bethel is named twice. So is Beersheba.
And in Exodus, God tells Moses: by my name Yahweh, I was not known to them. Meaning Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
But back in Genesis chapter four, people had already begun to call on Yahweh's name.
The strongest evidence is the flood.

Read it straight through and it trips over itself. Noah takes two of every kind of animal. Then seven pairs of every clean animal. Rain falls for forty days. The waters prevail for a hundred and fifty.
Now pull the verses apart, the way scholars do, using the name for God, the vocabulary, and the details.
You don't get scraps. You get two nearly complete flood stories. Each has a beginning, a middle, and an end, and each mostly reads on its own.
In one, Yahweh regrets making humankind. Noah takes seven pairs of the clean animals. It rains for forty days. And Yahweh smells the pleasant aroma of the sacrifice.
In the other, God sees that all flesh is corrupt. Noah takes two of each kind. The flood runs on a calendar, dated to the day, for about a year. And God sets his bow in the cloud, as a covenant.
Somebody had two flood stories. And instead of choosing one, they braided them together.
By the late eighteen hundreds, scholars had turned this into a theory. Its classic form came from the German scholar Julius Wellhausen. It's called the Documentary Hypothesis.
Four sources. Four letters.
J, the Yahwist, from the German spelling of Yahweh. Vivid storytelling. A God who walks in the garden in the cool of the day. Placed in the southern kingdom of Judah.
E, the Elohist. It calls God Elohim until Moses. Dreams, angels, prophets. Placed in the northern kingdom of Israel.
D, the Deuteronomist. The book of Deuteronomy: long speeches, one God, worshipped at one place.
And P, the Priestly source. Genealogies, dates, measurements, ritual law, and a God who creates by speaking. Genesis chapter one is P.
The theory tied each one to a moment in history.
In 722 BCE, Assyria destroys the northern kingdom. Northern traditions move south, and E is joined to J.

Around 622, during repairs to the Temple, the Bible says the high priest found a scroll: the Book of the Law. Since the early eighteen hundreds, scholars have argued it was an early form of Deuteronomy, written not long before it was found.
In 587, Babylon destroys Jerusalem. During and after the exile, priests shape P.
And last, an editor, the Redactor, weaves the strands into one. The Bible itself remembers a scene: Ezra the scribe, reading the Torah aloud to the people in Jerusalem.
J, E, D, P. For about a century, that was the dominant answer in critical scholarship.
Here's the part most explainers skip. The tidy four-letter version did not survive intact.
Beginning in the 1970s, scholars like John Van Seters, Hans Heinrich Schmid and Rolf Rendtorff, and later Erhard Blum, started pulling on the threads.
E proved hard to find as one continuous story. Many scholars now doubt it ever was one.
J was dated later, or broken into smaller blocks. Much European scholarship now simply divides the text into Priestly and non-Priestly material, and asks how it grew, layer by layer.
One influential proposal: the story of the ancestors and the story of the Exodus began as two separate accounts of where Israel came from, and were first joined by Priestly writers.

Meanwhile, a group of scholars in the United States and Israel, sometimes called the Neo-Documentarians, defend continuous sources, identified less by God's names than by whether the plot holds together.
So there is a real debate. But among academic biblical scholars, there is also a lot of agreement.
The Torah is composite. Many hands, over several centuries.
The Priestly material is real and recognizable. It's one of the most secure results in the field.
Deuteronomy is its own distinct voice, and most scholars tie its core to the seventh century BCE, and King Josiah's reforms.

And the five books reached something close to their final form in the Persian period, around the fifth or fourth century BCE. The oldest surviving scrolls of the books, among the Dead Sea Scrolls, date to about 250 BCE.
Go back to the flood. Somebody had two stories that disagreed about the animals, the rain, and the calendar. They could have picked one. They could have smoothed the seams.
They kept both.
Maybe out of reverence. Maybe to hold two communities together. We don't know.
But the result is a book that isn't one voice. It's a conversation, kept on purpose, where you can still hear more than one person talking.
